section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: In data parallelism with W workers, what does each worker hold and process during a training step?
options: A 1/W slice of the model's layers and the full global batch
A 1/W slice of each weight matrix and a 1/W shard of the batch
A complete copy of the model and the full global batch, processed redundantly
A complete copy of the model and a 1/W shard of the global batch
explanation: Data parallelism replicates the full model on every worker and splits each global batch into W shards, one per worker. The workers then average their per-shard gradients with an all-reduce. Splitting layers or weight matrices across workers is model (pipeline or tensor) parallelism, not data parallelism.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: In data parallelism, why do all W workers apply the identical optimizer update each step?
options: Because each worker's shard happens to produce the same local gradient
Because worker 0 computes the update and broadcasts new weights to the others
Because the optimizer state is shared in one memory location across GPUs
Because an all-reduce gives every worker the same averaged gradient before the step
explanation: Each worker computes a different local gradient from its own shard, but the all-reduce replaces every local gradient with the common average. Since every worker starts with identical weights and applies the identical averaged gradient, they stay identical. No weight broadcast is needed after the step.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: How many communication steps does ring all-reduce take for W workers, and how much of the tensor does each link carry per step?
options: 2(W-1) steps, each carrying 1/W of the tensor
W steps, each carrying the full tensor
W-1 steps, each carrying 2/W of the tensor
log2(W) steps, each carrying half the tensor
explanation: Ring all-reduce runs a reduce-scatter phase of W-1 steps followed by an all-gather phase of W-1 steps, for 2(W-1) steps total. On every step each link carries exactly one chunk, which is 1/W of the tensor. That keeps per-worker traffic near 2 tensors' worth regardless of W.

section: Prerequisites / You will learn / Why this matters
question: Why is data parallelism described as the foundation for the rest of a distributed-training toolkit (ZeRO, FSDP, tensor/pipeline parallelism)?
options: Because those strategies replace the training loop entirely and only reuse its data loader
Because those strategies require the model to be replicated unchanged on every worker
Because those strategies are all built on top of the same collective-communication operations
Because those strategies only work when the global batch fits on one GPU
explanation: Data parallelism introduces the collective (all-reduce, and its parts reduce-scatter and all-gather) that coordinates devices. ZeRO, FSDP and tensor/pipeline parallelism are all built on top of these collectives. ZeRO and FSDP in particular specifically stop replicating the full model state, so they do not require unchanged replication.

question: A NumPy example simulates data parallelism with a Python loop that plays all W workers in one process. What does such a simulation demonstrate?
options: The wall-clock speedup to expect when the same job runs on W real GPUs
The network bandwidth an all-reduce of the gradients would consume on NVLink
The arithmetic of gradient averaging and all-reduce, not a multi-GPU speedup
How much gradient computation and communication overlap on real multi-GPU hardware
explanation: A single-process loop executes each simulated worker in turn, so it reproduces the numbers the collective produces but cannot run anything in parallel. It therefore says nothing about speedup, bandwidth, or overlap. Those require real multi-GPU hardware.

section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
question: What is the correct order of the four things data parallelism does every training step?
options: Shard the batch, all-reduce the inputs, compute local gradients, replicate the update
Replicate the model, compute the full-batch gradient, shard it, all-reduce the weights
Replicate the model, shard the batch, compute local gradients, all-reduce the gradients
Shard the model, replicate the batch, all-reduce activations, compute gradients
explanation: Every worker holds an identical replica, the global batch is cut into W shards, each worker runs forward and backward on its shard to get a local gradient, and an all-reduce averages those gradients across workers. Then each worker runs the identical optimizer step. The all-reduce operates on gradients, not inputs, activations, or weights.

section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
question: With a global batch of B examples split across W data-parallel workers, how many examples does each worker's local gradient come from?
options: B/W examples
B examples
W examples
B times W examples
explanation: The global batch of B examples is cut into W equal shards, so each worker processes B/W examples and computes its local gradient from them. The all-reduce then combines the W local gradients into one gradient that reflects all B examples.

section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
question: What does an all-reduce do?
options: Combines one tensor from every worker and returns the combined result to all of them
Sends one worker's tensor, unchanged, to every other worker in the group
Combines one tensor from every worker and leaves the combined result only on worker 0
Splits one tensor into equal pieces and gives each worker a different piece of it
explanation: An all-reduce takes an equally shaped tensor from every worker, combines them element-wise (for data parallelism, by averaging), and leaves the same combined result on every worker. Sending one tensor unchanged to everyone is a broadcast; leaving the result on one worker is a reduce; giving each worker a different piece is a scatter.

section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
question: Why do data-parallel workers remain bit-for-bit identical across training steps?
options: They periodically compare weights and roll back any worker that drifted
They start identical and every step applies the same averaged update
They all process the same shard of data each step
They share one set of weights stored on worker 0
explanation: Workers begin with identical weights and, after the all-reduce, each applies exactly the same averaged gradient with the same optimizer. Identical inputs to identical updates give identical outputs, so the replicas never diverge. They process different data, which is why their local gradients differ before averaging.

section: 1. Intuition: clone the model, split the batch, agree on the update
question: Relative to a single-GPU training loop, what is the one new operation that data parallelism introduces?
options: An all-reduce of the gradients
A second backward pass per step
A new optimizer that accepts W gradients
A broadcast of the loss value after each step
explanation: Data parallelism runs the same loop on W workers, each on different data. The only new step is the all-reduce that averages gradients across workers. The optimizer is unchanged, and the loss value is not what is synchronized.

section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
question: Is data-parallel training with gradient averaging an approximation of full-batch training or an exact equivalent?
options: An approximation whose error shrinks as the number of workers W grows
Exactly equal to the full-batch gradient, for a mean loss and equal shards
An approximation whose error shrinks as the global batch size B grows larger
Exactly equal, but only when W is a power of two so the shards stay balanced
explanation: For a mean loss and equal-size shards, the average of per-shard mean-loss gradients equals the full-batch mean-loss gradient exactly, as an algebraic identity. Only floating-point reduction order can cause tiny numerical differences. There is no approximation error that depends on W or batch size.

section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
question: A worker computes the gradient of the mean loss over its shard of B/W examples. Why does its local gradient carry a factor of W/B in front of the sum of per-example gradients?
options: Because the gradient is pre-scaled by W so that it cancels the later averaging over workers
Because the shard mean divides by the shard size B/W, which equals multiplying by W/B
Because the learning rate is divided by B on each worker before the gradient is formed
Because each example is counted W times in total across all of the workers' shards
explanation: A mean over a shard of B/W examples divides the sum by B/W, which is the same as multiplying by W/B. When the W local gradients are then averaged (multiplied by 1/W), the W cancels and leaves 1/B times the sum over all examples, which is the full-batch gradient.

section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
question: In the proof that averaged shard gradients equal the full-batch gradient, why does the double sum over workers and over each worker's indices collapse into one sum over all B examples?
options: Because the shards overlap, so each example is counted once on average
Because gradients of different examples are orthogonal
Because the shards partition the batch: every example is in exactly one shard
Because the per-example losses are all equal at initialization
explanation: The shards are disjoint and together cover the whole batch, so summing over workers and then over each worker's examples visits every example exactly once. That makes the double sum identical to a single sum over all B examples. Overlapping shards would double-count examples and break the identity.

section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
question: Which two conditions does the exact equality 'average of per-shard gradients = full-batch gradient' require?
options: A sum loss and an even number of workers
Identical shards and a sum loss
A convex loss and a learning rate below 1
A mean loss and equal-size shards
explanation: The proof relies on each worker's loss being a mean over its shard and on all shards having the same size, so that a plain average over workers gives the global mean. With a sum loss or unequal shards, a plain average no longer reproduces the full-batch mean-loss gradient. Convexity and the learning rate play no role.

section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
question: If data-parallel shards have unequal sizes, how should per-worker mean-loss gradients be combined to recover the full-batch mean-loss gradient?
options: A size-weighted average, weighting each worker by its share of the examples
A plain sum over workers, since each shard mean is already normalized
A plain average over workers, exactly as with equal-size shards
Keep only the gradient from the largest shard and broadcast it to all workers
explanation: With unequal shards, each worker's mean already divides by its own size, so a plain average over-weights examples in small shards. Weighting each worker's gradient by its share of the examples restores the global mean. A plain sum would scale the gradient by roughly W.

section: 2. The correctness fact: averaging shard gradients == the full-batch gradient
question: Why does the data-parallel all-reduce use an average rather than a sum of the per-worker gradients?
options: Because the averaged gradient has lower variance than the sum, which is what stabilizes training
Because averaging per-shard mean-loss gradients reproduces the full-batch mean-loss gradient
Because NCCL only supports averaging collectives, not sums, for floating-point tensors
Because summing W fp32 gradient tensors would overflow the fp32 range for large W
explanation: Each worker's gradient is from a mean loss over its shard. Averaging W such gradients gives exactly the full-batch mean-loss gradient, while summing them gives a gradient W times larger. Collective libraries support sums; averaging is a sum followed by division by W.

question: For the mean-squared-error loss (1/n) sum_i (x_i . theta - y_i)^2 used in a linear-regression check of data parallelism, what is the closed-form gradient with respect to theta?
options: (1/n) X^T (X theta - y)
2 X^T (X theta - y)
(2/n) X^T (X theta - y)
(2/n) (X theta - y)^T X theta
explanation: Differentiating (1/n) times the sum of squared residuals gives 2/n times X transposed times the residual vector (X theta - y). The factor 1/n comes from the mean, and the factor 2 from differentiating the square. Dropping the 1/n would give the gradient of a sum loss instead.

question: A NumPy check of data parallelism finds the maximum absolute difference between the full-batch gradient and the average of four shard gradients is about 2.2e-16. What does this show?
options: The two gradients differ by a small approximation error that grows with the number of workers W
The shard gradients were computed in fp16, so they lost precision relative to the full batch
The two gradients are equal up to floating-point noise, i.e. exactly equal mathematically
The averaged gradient is slightly biased toward the first shard, which is reduced first
explanation: A difference around 2.2e-16 is at the level of double-precision machine epsilon, which is pure floating-point rounding. It confirms the algebraic identity: the averaged shard gradient equals the full-batch gradient. It is not an approximation error that depends on the number of workers.

question: Training uses a per-token mean loss on variable-length sequences with padding, so data-parallel workers have different numbers of valid tokens. What is wrong with a plain average of worker gradients?
options: Nothing: per-token mean losses always make a plain average over workers exact
It double-counts the padding tokens, so padding gradients must be summed instead of averaged
It is subtly wrong; each worker's gradient must be weighted by its share of the valid tokens
It is only wrong if W is odd, since an even split always balances the valid tokens
explanation: A plain average assumes each worker contributes equally to the global mean. When valid-token counts differ, the global token-mean gradient is sum(n_w * g_w) / sum(n_w), so each worker must be weighted by its token count. Ignoring this silently changes how much each token contributes.

question: What symptom does getting the data-parallel gradient normalization wrong (for example, using a sum loss with a plain average) typically produce?
options: An immediate crash in the all-reduce with a tensor shape mismatch error
An effective learning rate that depends on the number of workers W
Workers whose weights slowly diverge from each other over many steps
A deadlock in the all-reduce once the gradient values grow too large
explanation: If the gradient is scaled by a factor that depends on W, the step size the optimizer actually takes scales with W too, so changing the worker count silently changes the effective learning rate. This is a classic silent scaling bug: no error is raised, and the replicas still stay identical because they all use the same wrong gradient.

question: What property must the element-wise combine operation of an all-reduce have, so that partial results can be combined in any grouping?
options: It must be idempotent
It must be associative
It must be invertible
It must be linear in the learning rate
explanation: An all-reduce combines tensors from many workers in some order and grouping chosen by the algorithm, so the operation must be associative (sum, max, and so on). For data parallelism the op is a sum, followed by division by W to get the mean. Idempotence or invertibility are not required.

question: Which of these is a family of collective communication operations that coordinate many devices at once?
options: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast
forward, backward, optimizer.step, zero_grad
fork, join, mutex, semaphore, condition variable, barrier
map, filter, sort, shuffle, partition, group-by
explanation: Collective communication operations involve all participating devices together: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, and broadcast are the standard members. Ring all-reduce itself is built from a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. The other options are training-loop steps or generic programming primitives.

question: In a naive all-reduce where every worker sends its tensor to worker 0, which sums and sends the result back, what is the problem?
options: The result is numerically different from a true sum because of the reduction order at worker 0
Workers other than worker 0 never receive the summed result, so they cannot step
Worker 0's link carries W-1 tensors in and W-1 out, a bottleneck that worsens as W grows
It only works when W is a power of two, so arbitrary GPU counts cannot use it
explanation: The naive scheme is correct but funnels all traffic through worker 0: it receives W-1 tensors and sends W-1 back. With gradients of hundreds of megabytes and hundreds of workers, that single link becomes a fatal bottleneck. Ring all-reduce avoids routing everything through one node.

question: In ring all-reduce, which workers does worker w send to?
options: Every other worker, in parallel
Only worker 0
Worker w+1 in reduce-scatter and worker w-1 in all-gather, plus worker 0
Only worker w+1, wrapping around at the end
explanation: Ring all-reduce arranges workers in a logical ring: worker w sends only to its right neighbour w+1, with the last worker wrapping to worker 0. No node handles all the traffic. Every link carries the same small amount per step.

question: Before ring all-reduce starts exchanging data, how does each worker divide its tensor?
options: Into 2 halves
Into W-1 chunks
Into W chunks
Into one chunk per layer
explanation: Each worker splits its tensor into W chunks (near-equal when the length does not divide evenly). Each step of the ring moves one chunk per link. After the reduce-scatter phase, each worker owns one fully summed chunk.

question: What is the state at the end of the reduce-scatter phase of ring all-reduce (after W-1 steps)?
options: Every worker already holds the full summed tensor, all W chunks
Each worker holds the fully summed value of one distinct chunk
Worker 0 holds the full sum and the other workers hold nothing
Each worker still holds its original tensor, with nothing summed yet
explanation: During reduce-scatter, each worker repeatedly sends one chunk to its right neighbour and adds the chunk it receives into its own buffer. After W-1 steps each worker has the complete sum for exactly one distinct chunk: the sum is 'scattered' across workers. The all-gather phase then spreads those finished chunks to everyone.

question: What happens during the all-gather phase of ring all-reduce?
options: Each worker adds the chunks it receives into its own buffer to finish the partial sums
The finished chunks are passed around the ring until every worker has all W of them
Worker 0 broadcasts the full summed result to all the other workers in one step
Each worker discards all chunks except its own finished chunk and divides by W
explanation: After reduce-scatter, each worker owns one finished chunk. The all-gather phase circulates these finished chunks around the ring for W-1 steps until every worker holds all W finished chunks. It copies results rather than adding them.

question: Over a whole ring all-reduce, roughly how much data does each worker send, as W grows large?
options: About W tensors' worth, one per other worker
About log2(W) tensors' worth, as in a tree
About 1/W of a tensor, its own chunk only
About 2 tensors' worth, independent of W
explanation: Each worker sends one chunk (1/W of the tensor) per step over 2(W-1) steps, which totals 2(W-1)/W, approaching 2 tensors' worth regardless of W. This is why ring all-reduce is called bandwidth-optimal. The naive scheme instead piles 2(W-1) tensors onto one link.

question: Why is ring all-reduce called bandwidth-optimal?
options: Because per-worker data stays about 2 tensors regardless of W, and no single link is a bottleneck
Because it finishes in a constant number of communication steps, regardless of how large W gets
Because it compresses the gradients to a lower precision before sending them around the whole ring
Because it only sends the nonzero entries of the gradient, which cuts the bytes on every link
explanation: Each link carries only 1/W of the tensor per step, and the total each worker moves stays near 2 tensors' worth however many workers there are. No link carries more than its share. Its number of rounds, 2(W-1), still grows with W, so latency is not constant.

section: Worked example: three workers, by hand
question: In ring all-reduce with three workers holding [1,2,3], [4,5,6] and [7,8,9], what does each worker hold at the end of the full all-reduce with op='mean'?
explanation: The element-wise sum is [12, 15, 18]; dividing by W = 3 gives the mean [4, 5, 6], which every worker ends up holding. [12, 15, 18] is the op='sum' result. [6, 15, 24] would be per-worker sums, which is not what an all-reduce computes.

section: Worked example: three workers, by hand
question: In the second reduce-scatter step of a ring all-reduce, which chunk does worker i send onward?
options: Its own original chunk i again, unchanged from the start
A random chunk chosen by the ring scheduler each step
The chunk it just updated in the previous step, (i-1) mod W
Chunk 0 always, which every worker forwards first in each step
explanation: On each reduce-scatter step a worker forwards the chunk it just accumulated into, which for step 1 is chunk (i-1) mod W. That keeps partial sums moving around the ring and growing by one contribution per hop. After W-1 hops each chunk has collected all W contributions on one worker.

section: Worked example: three workers, by hand
question: In a three-worker ring all-reduce of [1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7,8,9], after reduce-scatter which finished chunk does each worker own?
options: Worker 0 owns chunk 0 (12), worker 1 owns chunk 1 (15), worker 2 owns chunk 2 (18)
Worker 0 owns all three chunks; workers 1 and 2 own none
Worker 0 owns chunk 1 (15), worker 1 owns chunk 2 (18), worker 2 owns chunk 0 (12)
Worker 0 owns chunk 2 (18), worker 1 owns chunk 0 (12), worker 2 owns chunk 1 (15)
explanation: Tracing the ring, worker 0 finishes chunk 1 (2+13 = 15), worker 1 finishes chunk 2 (6+12 = 18), and worker 2 finishes chunk 0 (7+5 = 12). Together they are the true sum [12, 15, 18], scattered one per worker. All-gather then distributes them so everyone holds the full result.

question: In a simulated ring all-reduce, each round first copies every worker's outgoing chunk into a 'sent' list before any worker adds. Why?
options: So no worker reads a neighbour's already-updated value mid-step, mirroring simultaneous sends
To save memory by reusing the same send buffers across all rounds instead of allocating new ones
To convert the chunks to fp16 before sending, halving the bytes that travel around the ring
So that the whole reduce-scatter phase can be skipped when there is only one worker, W = 1
explanation: On real hardware all workers send at the same moment from the state they had at the start of the step. In a sequential loop, updating worker i before worker i+1 reads from it would leak updated values into the same round. Snapshotting the outgoing chunks first reproduces the simultaneous semantics.

question: In a ring all-reduce implementation, why does the reduce-scatter phase add received chunks while the all-gather phase overwrites with them?
options: Reduce-scatter combines partial sums; all-gather only copies already finished results around
Adding is faster during the first phase and overwriting is faster during the second phase
All-gather must undo the additions made during reduce-scatter, so that each chunk is counted only once
Overwriting during all-gather is what converts the accumulated sum into the final mean
explanation: During reduce-scatter each chunk accumulates contributions from all workers, so received data must be added. During all-gather the chunks are already fully summed, so a worker just copies the finished chunk into place. Adding during all-gather would double-count and give wrong results. The mean comes from a separate division by W.

question: Why does a ring all-reduce implementation compute W near-equal chunk bounds rather than assuming the tensor length divides by W?
options: So it works for tensor lengths that do not divide evenly by the number of workers
Because NCCL requires chunks of different sizes for each worker position in the ring
So that the last worker receives an empty chunk and can skip communication
Because the first chunk must be twice as large to hold the running partial sums
explanation: Real gradient tensors rarely have a length that is an exact multiple of W. Near-equal chunk bounds let the algorithm split any length into W pieces whose sizes differ by at most one element. The accompanying tests specifically cover lengths that do not divide evenly.

question: Why is a ring all-reduce implementation tested against np.sum and np.mean for worker counts 1 to 8 and uneven tensor lengths?
options: Because ring all-reduce is only approximate and needs a tolerance check against exact sums
Because ring all-reduce only works for even W, and the odd counts must be shown to fail
Because NumPy uses a different reduction order for each worker count, so results must be compared
Because the reduce-scatter/all-gather index arithmetic is fiddly and easy to get off by one
explanation: The schedule of which chunk each worker sends on each step is easy to get subtly wrong by one position. Comparing the ring's output to a direct sum or mean across many worker counts and awkward lengths catches such off-by-one errors. If you re-derive the schedule, the test protects you.

section: 5. Tying it back to the training loop: data_parallel_grads
question: In data-parallel training, what does the ring all-reduce combine?
options: Gradients, before the optimizer changes the weights
Model predictions from different workers
Training examples from different workers
Updated weights, after each worker's optimizer step
explanation: Data parallelism all-reduces the .grad tensors produced by backward, before optimizer.step() runs. It does not move examples, predictions, or updated weights. Averaging weights after independent local updates would be a different (and here incorrect) algorithm.

section: Follow one optimizer step, with actual numbers
question: Three data-parallel workers start with the same parameters and compute different local gradients. After all-reduce and SGD, why do they hold the same new parameters without exchanging weights?
options: Because SGD is invariant to the gradient value, so any gradient gives the same step
Because each worker's local gradient was already equal to the global average beforehand
Because worker 0 sends its updated weights to all the other workers after each step
Because all workers apply the same averaged gradient to the same starting weights
explanation: The all-reduce replaces each worker's local gradient with the common average, and every worker starts from identical parameters. Applying theta_new = theta_old - lr * g_avg on each worker therefore gives identical results. No weight broadcast is needed after the step.

section: Follow one optimizer step, with actual numbers
question: If data-parallel workers use Adam instead of SGD, what additional condition is needed for their weights to stay identical?
options: Nothing; Adam is stateless
Each worker must use a different learning rate
A separate all-reduce of the updated weights after every step
Matching optimizer state and settings on every worker
explanation: Adam keeps per-parameter moment buffers and hyperparameters. Identical averaged gradients only yield identical updates if every worker also has the same moment state and settings. Starting from the same state and applying the same gradients keeps that state identical too.

section: Follow one optimizer step, with actual numbers
question: Which action in a data-parallel training step actually changes the model's parameters?
options: loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
The gradient all-reduce
optimizer.zero_grad()
explanation: backward() computes gradients into .grad, and the all-reduce makes those gradients agree across workers, but neither touches the parameters. Only optimizer.step() reads .grad and updates the parameters. zero_grad() only resets gradients.

question: In a manual data-parallel training step, where should the gradient all-reduce be inserted?
options: Before the forward pass, so every worker starts the step from synchronized gradients
After local backward and before gradient clipping and optimizer.step()
After optimizer.step() and before the next forward, so the new weights get averaged
Between gradient clipping and optimizer.step(), so each local gradient is clipped first
explanation: Local backward first fills each parameter's .grad, then the all-reduce averages them, then clipping and the optimizer act on the averaged gradient. Synchronizing after the step is too late because the workers would already have diverged. Clipping before averaging gives a different result because clipping is nonlinear.

question: A manual data-parallel loop calls dist.all_reduce(parameter.grad, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM) and then parameter.grad.div_(world_size). What is the purpose of the division?
options: To normalize by the number of parameters
To reduce the learning rate for stability
To undo the in-place modification made by all_reduce
To convert the sum into the mean gradient
explanation: The SUM all-reduce leaves the sum of all workers' gradients in .grad. Dividing in place by world_size turns that sum into the mean, which is the gradient equal to the full-batch mean-loss gradient. Without it the gradient would be W times too large.

question: How does torch.distributed.all_reduce deliver its result?
options: It returns a new result tensor and leaves the input tensor unchanged on every process
It writes the result only into rank 0's tensor, leaving the others with their local values
It modifies the supplied tensor in place on every participating process
It stores the result in a separate pinned buffer on the CPU that each process must read
explanation: all_reduce overwrites the tensor you pass on each process. For example, worker 0's .grad [1, 2, 3] becomes the sum [12, 15, 18] after a three-worker SUM all-reduce, and dividing by 3 gives [4, 5, 6]. The optimizer then reads that updated .grad.

question: Does data-parallel training require a special optimizer that understands multiple workers?
options: Yes; it needs a special optimizer that accepts all W gradients
No; the ordinary optimizer reads the already averaged .grad
Yes; it needs an optimizer that broadcasts updated weights
Only if the model has more than one layer of parameters
explanation: After the all-reduce, each parameter's .grad already holds the averaged gradient. The ordinary optimizer just reads .grad and updates its local copy as usual. Synchronization happens entirely in the gradient step.

question: A manual data-parallel loop iterates 'for parameter in model.parameters(): dist.all_reduce(parameter.grad, ...)'. What does each iteration of that loop correspond to?
options: One worker process in the data-parallel group of W
One micro-batch of the gradient accumulation window
One training example from this worker's shard of data
One parameter tensor, such as a layer's weight or bias
explanation: The loop walks over parameter tensors, not workers; every worker runs the same loop. A linear layer has a weight tensor and a bias tensor, so it causes two collective calls. The other workers participate by making matching calls in the same order.

question: Across processes participating in manual gradient all-reduces, what must agree for the collectives to work correctly?
options: Their random seeds for dropout and data shuffling
Tensor shapes, types, and the order of collective calls
Their local loss values at the end of each step
Their data shards, which must contain the same examples
explanation: Collectives pair up tensors across processes by call order, so every process must issue the same sequence of calls with matching shapes and dtypes (weights with weights, biases with biases). Losses, dropout masks, and data shards are expected to differ across workers.

question: What goes wrong if each data-parallel worker calls optimizer.step() on its local gradient and the gradients are averaged afterward?
options: The workers have already made different updates, so their weights diverge
Nothing; the order of stepping and averaging does not matter at all for plain SGD
The all-reduce fails because .grad was already cleared by the step
The learning rate ends up applied twice to the same averaged gradient
explanation: If each worker steps on its own local gradient, the replicas apply different updates and their weights no longer match. Averaging gradients afterward cannot undo that. The all-reduce must come before the step so everyone uses the same gradient.

question: In data-parallel training, why should gradient clipping be applied after averaging rather than to each local gradient?
options: Because clipping is nonlinear, so clipping local gradients first generally gives a different result
Because clipping before averaging is mathematically identical but needs W separate norm computations
Because local gradients are always below the clip threshold, so clipping them would do nothing
Because the all-reduce itself clips the gradients, so only the averaged result needs checking
explanation: Clipping rescales a gradient based on its norm, which is nonlinear: the average of clipped gradients is not the clipped average. To clip the gradient the optimizer actually uses, average first and then clip. The all-reduce does not clip anything.

question: A helper data_parallel_grads(grad_fn, params, batch, world_size) splits the batch, computes a gradient per shard, and ring-all-reduces them with op='mean'. What does it return?
options: Updated parameters after one SGD step on the batch
The mean loss over the batch, averaged across shards
A list of W per-shard gradients, one for each worker
One averaged gradient; it does not update params
explanation: The helper only produces the gradient: it splits the batch into world_size equal shards, calls grad_fn on each, and averages them with a ring all-reduce. Updating parameters is a separate step, for example theta = theta - lr * grad. Keeping gradient computation and the update separate mirrors the real training loop.

question: In data_parallel_grads(grad_fn, params, batch, world_size), what must grad_fn(params, shard) compute?
options: The gradient of the sum loss over the whole batch at the given parameters
The updated parameters after one optimizer step taken on that shard
The gradient of the mean loss on that shard at the given parameters
The scalar loss value on the shard, which the helper then differentiates
explanation: grad_fn must return the gradient of the mean loss over its shard at the current parameters. Averaging those mean-loss gradients over equal shards gives the full-batch mean-loss gradient. A sum-loss gradient would make the result scale with shard size.

question: A single-process simulation of data parallelism returns just one copy of the averaged gradient. What does it reproduce, and what does it not?
options: It reproduces the parallel execution but not the arithmetic
It reproduces both the arithmetic and the parallel speedup
It reproduces the arithmetic, not the parallel execution
It reproduces neither; it is only a placeholder
explanation: One Python process computes each shard's gradient in turn and the ring helper returns one copy because all simulated workers' buffers agree. That reproduces the numbers exactly. On real GPUs each process keeps its own copy of the averaged gradient and updates its own model concurrently.

section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
question: What does 'torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=4 train.py' start on a machine with four GPUs?
options: One Python process that loops over the four GPUs, running each shard in turn
Four threads sharing one model and one optimizer inside a single Python process
Four Python processes running the same file, each with its own model, optimizer and GPU
One process per layer of the model, each pinned to one of the four GPUs in a pipeline
explanation: torchrun launches four separate Python processes, each running train.py with its own model replica, optimizer, Python variables, and assigned GPU. Each process is one worker. There is no single process looping over the GPUs.

section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
question: In PyTorch distributed training, what do world_size, rank, and local_rank mean?
options: world_size = total processes; rank = this process's ID in the whole group; local_rank = its GPU index on its machine
world_size = GPUs per machine; rank = index of this machine in the job; local_rank = index of the layer this process owns
world_size = number of machines; rank = this process's GPU index; local_rank = index of the thread inside the process
world_size = global batch size; rank = index of the current micro-batch; local_rank = index of this worker's data shard
explanation: world_size is the total number of processes in the job, rank uniquely identifies a process across the whole job, and local_rank is the GPU index of that process on its own machine. On one four-GPU machine rank and local_rank coincide (0 to 3).

section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
question: In a multi-machine data-parallel job, how do global ranks and local ranks behave?
options: Both restart at zero on each machine, so ranks repeat across machines
Global ranks are unique across the job; local ranks start at zero on each machine
Global ranks start at zero on each machine; local ranks are unique across the job
Both are unique across the job, so local rank always equals global rank
explanation: The global rank is a unique ID for every process in the whole job, while the local rank indexes GPUs on one machine, so it restarts at zero on every machine. A process uses local_rank to pick its GPU and rank to identify itself in collectives.

section: What “one process per GPU” actually means
question: On a four-GPU data-parallel job with a global batch of 32, how is backward executed?
options: One process runs backward four times in a loop, once for each GPU's 8-example shard
Four processes each run one local backward on 8 examples concurrently and join the collectives
One process runs backward on all 32 examples and then broadcasts the gradients to the other GPUs
Each of the four processes runs backward on all 32 examples redundantly and keeps its own result
explanation: Each of the four processes handles its own 8-example shard and performs one local backward, at the same time as the others, then participates in the gradient collectives. No process loops over the other GPUs' backward calls.

question: With micro-batch size b, A accumulation steps per optimizer update, and W data-parallel workers, how many examples does one optimizer update cover?
options: b times A
b times A divided by W
b times (A + W)
b times A times W
explanation: Each worker processes A micro-batches of b examples before the update, and W workers contribute, so the global batch is b * A * W. For b = 2, A = 4, W = 3, that is 24 examples per update. Changing any of the three factors changes the global batch.

question: When combining gradient accumulation over A equal micro-batches with data parallelism over W workers, how is the overall averaging achieved for mean losses?
options: Divide each micro-batch loss by A·W before backward and then use a plain sum all-reduce instead
No division is needed at all; gradient accumulation averages the micro-batches automatically
Divide the learning rate by A and the gradient by W, so the two factors are applied separately
Divide each micro-batch loss by A before backward; the worker average supplies the 1/W factor
explanation: Backward adds into .grad, so dividing each micro-batch's mean loss by A makes the accumulated gradient an average over the accumulation window. The data-parallel all-reduce then averages across workers, contributing the separate 1/W. Without the 1/A, the accumulated gradient would be A times too large.

question: What is the distinction between gradient accumulation and data parallelism?
options: Accumulation combines work across workers; data parallelism combines work over time on each single worker
Both combine work across workers, but accumulation uses a sum while data parallelism uses a mean
Accumulation combines work over time on each worker; data parallelism combines work across workers
Accumulation changes the model's effective depth; data parallelism changes the optimizer's state
explanation: Gradient accumulation adds several micro-batches' gradients on one worker over successive backward passes. Data parallelism averages gradients computed concurrently on different workers. In both, optimizer.step() runs only once the intended combined gradient is ready.

question: What is NCCL?
options: A file format for sharded checkpoints written by each GPU in a distributed job
A PyTorch module that shards the input batch across GPUs and chooses which data each one sees
A compiler that fuses CUDA kernels across GPUs to reduce launch overhead
NVIDIA's Collective Communications Library, which runs collectives across NVIDIA GPUs
explanation: NCCL (pronounced 'nickel') is NVIDIA's library of GPU collective communication operations such as all-reduce and all-gather. PyTorch distributed uses it as the backend that actually moves and combines tensors between GPUs. It does not choose data or shard batches.

question: In data-parallel training, which component is responsible for executing the collectives across NVIDIA GPUs over the available connections?
options: The training loop
The NCCL backend
PyTorch distributed / DDP
The optimizer
explanation: The training loop chooses data, computes the loss, requests backward, and runs the optimizer. PyTorch distributed and DDP coordinate processes and request gradient collectives. The NCCL backend executes those collectives across the GPUs using whatever links exist.

question: What does NCCL know about the training it supports?
options: It knows the loss value and adjusts the learning rate when gradients grow too large
It knows the model architecture and reorders layers to overlap their communication
It knows which examples each worker processed and reweights the workers' gradients by their counts
It knows tensors and collective operations, but nothing about examples, losses or learning rates
explanation: NCCL just combines corresponding entries of tensors as requested by a collective. The interpretation of the result as 'training on a larger batch' comes from the mean-loss definition and the averaging proof. NCCL itself has no notion of examples, losses, or learning rates.

question: Is the ring algorithm a requirement of the all-reduce operation used by NCCL?
options: No; ring is one implementation, and NCCL can pick other algorithms and transports with the same result
Yes; all-reduce is defined as the ring schedule, so any other algorithm would give a different result
Yes, but only across nodes; within one node NCCL must use NVLink broadcasts instead of an all-reduce
No; NCCL always uses a naive gather to rank 0 followed by a broadcast, and the ring is only a teaching aid
explanation: All-reduce is defined by its result, not its schedule. Ring is one implementation; NCCL can select other algorithms and transports depending on NVLink, PCIe, or network connections. The mathematical result is the same, apart from tiny floating-point differences caused by different reduction orders. NCCL does not always gather to rank 0.

question: A DDP script is run on a machine without CUDA. What backend does it use and what should you expect?
options: NCCL on the CPU, with the same speedup as on GPUs
Gloo on the CPU: correct results with no speedup
It cannot run at all without CUDA
MPI only, with approximate gradients
explanation: Without CUDA, the same DDP code can fall back to the Gloo backend on the CPU. It performs the same gradient averaging, so results are correct, but it is not faster. NCCL is specific to NVIDIA GPUs.

question: Which statement about GPU collective communication in data-parallel training is accurate?
options: It requires NVLink between GPUs and is always free, because copy engines handle all of it
It is GPU work scheduled on CUDA streams that may overlap computation; NVLink is not required
It runs only on the host CPU and never uses any GPU resources such as SMs or memory bandwidth
It can be measured precisely, including overlap and speedup, by a single-process CPU simulation
explanation: Collectives are GPU work scheduled on CUDA streams and may overlap computation, but they are not guaranteed to be a free transfer handled only by copy engines. NVLink improves bandwidth but is not required. A CPU simulation cannot measure this overlap or predict speedup.

section: 7. PyTorch DDP: overlapping the all-reduce with backward
question: What is PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel (DDP)?
options: A data loader that shards each batch across the GPUs in the job automatically
An optimizer that averages parameter updates across the GPUs
A wrapper around the model that arranges gradient synchronization during backward
A launcher that starts one Python process per GPU and sets each process's rank
explanation: DDP wraps a model and hooks into backward so that gradients are synchronized (averaged across ranks) as they become ready. It is not an optimizer, a data loader, or a launcher; torchrun launches processes and DistributedSampler chooses data.

section: What changes in the training step?
question: After wrapping a model with DistributedDataParallel, should you also add a manual loop that all-reduces each parameter's .grad and divides by world_size?
options: Yes; DDP only sums gradients across ranks, so the manual division by world_size is still needed
Only when using plain SGD, since adaptive optimizers like Adam normalize the gradient scale anyway
Yes; otherwise the optimizer on each rank would still see only its own local gradients
No; default DDP already averages gradients, and an extra all-reduce plus division would be wrong
explanation: Default DDP already averages gradients during backward. Adding the manual all-reduce loop would synchronize twice, and the extra division by W would shrink the gradient incorrectly. The manual loop only explains what DDP does.

section: What changes in the training step?
question: Which of these does DDP not do for you?
options: Average gradients across ranks during backward
Synchronize the starting model across ranks
Shard the input batch or call the optimizer
Group gradients into buckets for communication
explanation: DDP averages gradients, broadcasts the initial model state, and buckets gradients for overlapped communication. It does not decide which examples each rank sees (that is the data pipeline, e.g. DistributedSampler) and it does not call optimizer.step(). You still write those parts of the loop.

section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
question: Why can DDP begin communicating gradients before backward has finished?
options: Because DDP skips the gradients of early layers, which change slowly, and only sends later ones
Because DDP computes all of the gradients during the forward pass and caches them for the backward pass
Because the optimizer step can safely run on each layer before the rest of backward completes
Because backward produces later layers' gradients first, and those can be reduced while it continues
explanation: Backward runs in reverse order, so an output layer's gradients exist before an input layer's. Communicating the output layer's gradients does not require waiting for the rest. DDP launches the reduction for a ready bucket while backward continues on other layers.

section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
question: In DDP, what is a gradient bucket?
options: Exactly one layer's gradients, sent as soon as that layer's backward pass is done
A copy of the optimizer state for one parameter, kept in sync across ranks
A buffer holding the loss values from all ranks, reduced together once per step
A group of parameter gradients reduced together when ready; it need not be one layer
explanation: DDP groups parameter gradients into buckets and launches one reduction per bucket when all its gradients are ready. A bucket can hold several parameter tensors and does not have to align with a layer. Bucketing enables overlap and amortizes launch overhead.

section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
question: Three layers each take 4 ms of backward and each bucket takes 3 ms to communicate. With DDP-style overlap the step takes 15 ms rather than 21 ms. What does the remaining 3 ms beyond the 12 ms of computation represent?
options: Optimizer step time, which runs after backward and cannot overlap anything
Exposed communication: the last bucket's reduction cannot overlap any remaining backward
Launch overhead of the first bucket's collective, paid before any overlap starts
Time spent in the forward pass, which DDP counts as part of the training step
explanation: The first bucket's gradients become ready only after backward has computed them, and the last bucket (the input layer's) becomes ready when backward finishes, leaving nothing to overlap with. Its 3 ms of communication is still exposed. Overlap hides 6 ms here, not all 9 ms.

section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
question: What trade-off governs DDP bucket size?
options: Bucket size only affects correctness, not speed, since every gradient is reduced exactly once
Larger buckets use less memory for communication buffers, but they are slower to compute during backward
Smaller buckets always win, because they start earlier and launch overhead is negligible
Larger buckets cut launch overhead but become ready later; smaller ones start earlier but need more calls
explanation: Bucketing avoids paying collective-launch overhead for every tiny parameter tensor, so larger buckets mean fewer calls. But a larger bucket waits for more gradients, so its communication starts later. Real performance depends on both the computation and the interconnect.

section: Why communication can begin before backward finishes
question: What does DDP's communication/computation overlap achieve?
options: It makes the all-reduce disappear entirely, since all communication hides under backward
It starts reducing ready gradients while others are computed; leftover communication still finishes before step
It lets the optimizer run on partially reduced gradients, then corrects them after the next step
It removes the need for any collective after backward, because gradients are exchanged during forward
explanation: Overlap hides some communication under remaining backward computation, but it does not eliminate communication. Any communication still in flight at the end of backward must finish before the optimizer can use those gradients. It also cannot guarantee proportional speedup from more workers.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: In a DDP training script, what ensures that all ranks start from the same model weights, even if they initialized differently?
options: torch.manual_seed must be identical on every rank, otherwise training fails to start
The optimizer copies the weights from rank 0 to every other rank when it takes its first step
DDP synchronizes the starting model across ranks by default when the model is wrapped
DistributedSampler broadcasts rank 0's model weights when the first batch is drawn
explanation: When a model is wrapped in DistributedDataParallel, DDP synchronizes the initial model state across ranks by default. Setting a seed is still good practice but is not what guarantees identical starting weights. The optimizer and sampler do not move model weights.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: What is the role of DistributedSampler in a DDP training script?
options: It averages gradients across ranks after each backward
It launches one process per GPU and assigns each a rank
It chooses which dataset indices each rank processes
It shards the model's parameters across the GPUs
explanation: Every rank refers to the same logical dataset, and DistributedSampler selects a different subset of indices for each rank, so workers see different examples. DDP itself does not split data; the sampler does. Gradient averaging is DDP's job and launching is torchrun's.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: Why does a DDP training loop call sampler.set_epoch(epoch) at the start of each epoch?
options: To reset the learning-rate schedule at the start of each new training epoch
To produce a new shuffle each epoch that is coordinated across ranks
To change which GPU each rank uses, balancing load across epochs
To clear the DDP gradient buckets so the new epoch starts fresh
explanation: DistributedSampler shuffles using a seed combined with the epoch. Calling set_epoch changes that shuffle every epoch while keeping all ranks consistent, so their shards still partition the data. Without it, every epoch would repeat the same ordering.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: A DDP script sums each rank's batch losses into loss_sum and then calls dist.all_reduce(loss_sum) before rank 0 logs it. Why is that all-reduce needed?
options: Because DDP synchronizes gradients, not the Python loss variable, so a global loss must be aggregated
Because the optimizer needs the global loss value on every rank to compute its next parameter update
Because DDP requires one extra collective per epoch to keep the ranks' model replicas in sync
Because without it the gradients would not be averaged across the ranks during backward
explanation: DDP only synchronizes gradients; each rank's loss value stays local. To report a global mean loss you must aggregate it yourself, which this separate all-reduce does. It plays no role in gradient synchronization or the optimizer step.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: In a DDP script, why set drop_last=True on both DistributedSampler and the DataLoader?
options: To keep shard and batch sizes regular: the sampler drops examples to split evenly, the loader drops partial batches
To make the shuffle deterministic across ranks, so that every rank draws exactly the same sequence of batches each epoch
To skip the first batch of each epoch, which DDP uses for warmup and bucket construction on every rank
To prevent DDP from synchronizing the last batch of the epoch, which would otherwise deadlock the job
explanation: With drop_last on the sampler, examples that do not divide evenly among ranks are discarded rather than padded; without it the sampler can pad with repeated indices. With drop_last on the loader, incomplete final local batches are discarded. Together they keep every rank's batches the same size, which the equal-shard averaging assumes.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: A DDP script uses a local batch of 8 per rank and is launched with four ranks. How many examples contribute to each optimizer step?
options: 8 examples
16 examples
32 examples
128 examples
explanation: Each of four ranks processes a local batch of 8, and DDP averages their gradients into one update, so 8 * 4 = 32 examples contribute per optimizer step. Adding ranks while keeping the local batch fixed increases the global batch.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: A DDP script checks whether LOCAL_RANK is in the environment and raises an error if not. What does that check enforce?
options: That the script was launched by torchrun or an equivalent launcher, not plain 'python train.py'
That the machine has at least one CUDA GPU visible, since DDP cannot run on a CPU-only machine otherwise
That only rank 0 runs the training loop while the other ranks just serve gradients
That the dataset was downloaded to local disk on every machine before training starts
explanation: torchrun sets LOCAL_RANK (and RANK, WORLD_SIZE, etc.) for every process it launches. If it is missing, the script was probably started directly with python and has no process group to join. The error message tells the user to launch with torchrun.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: In a DDP script on a CUDA machine, why does each process call torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank) and check local_rank < torch.cuda.device_count()?
options: So that NCCL falls back to running its collectives on the CPU
So that all processes share GPU 0 and the other GPUs stay free
So that each local process uses its own distinct GPU
So that the model's layers are sharded across GPUs by local rank
explanation: Each process should own one GPU on its machine, selected by its local rank. The check fails fast if more local processes were launched than there are GPUs. With NCCL, one process per GPU is the standard arrangement.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: In a DDP script, what do dist.init_process_group and dist.destroy_process_group do?
options: They create the model replicas on each rank and delete them all at the end of training
They start the CUDA kernels on each GPU and stop them when training ends
They load the latest checkpoint on start-up and save a final checkpoint on exit
They connect the processes into a communication group and clean it up at the end
explanation: init_process_group connects the launched processes with the chosen backend (NCCL or Gloo) so collectives can run. destroy_process_group, placed in a finally block, releases those resources at the end even after errors. Launching processes is torchrun's job.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: In a DDP script's main(), exceptions are logged with the rank and then re-raised. Why re-raise instead of swallowing the error?
options: So that the other ranks continue training without this one
So the launcher can report the failure
So that DDP retries the step automatically
So that the process group is not destroyed
explanation: Logging with the rank identifies where the failure happened, and re-raising lets the launcher see the process failed and report it. Swallowing the error would hide the failure and could leave peers waiting in collectives. The finally block still destroys the process group.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: In a DDP run, which component is responsible for each job: launching processes, connecting them, choosing each rank's data, synchronizing model and gradients, updating the local replica?
options: DDP; torchrun; the optimizer; DistributedSampler; NCCL
torchrun; init_process_group; DistributedSampler; DDP; the optimizer
init_process_group; DDP; torchrun; the optimizer; DistributedSampler
The optimizer; DistributedSampler; DDP; torchrun; init_process_group
explanation: torchrun launches the processes, init_process_group connects them, DistributedSampler chooses each rank's indices, DDP synchronizes the model and gradients, and the optimizer updates the local replica. Keeping these roles separate helps locate bugs.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: On Windows, torchrun may fail with a libuv error in CPU builds. How can a DDP script still be launched with four ranks?
options: Set WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR, MASTER_PORT, RANK and LOCAL_RANK yourself and start four processes
Run 'python train.py' once and let DDP spawn the other three ranks automatically from inside its wrapper
Install the NCCL backend for Windows and rerun torchrun with the same arguments
Use a single process with world_size=4, so that one process plays all four ranks
explanation: torchrun just sets environment variables and starts processes. You can do the same manually: set WORLD_SIZE, MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT, and for each of four processes set RANK and LOCAL_RANK, then start them. The script then runs with Gloo on the CPU.

section: A complete, small DDP training script
question: When launching a Gloo DDP job on the CPU, each process prints a 'client socket has failed to connect' warning before training proceeds normally. What does it mean?
options: One rank crashed and the others are training alone
The process group failed and gradients are not being averaged
It is harmless: Gloo probing the machine's hostname
MASTER_PORT is wrong and must be changed
explanation: This warning comes from Gloo probing the hostname before falling back to a working address. It is harmless, and rank 0 then prints the falling epoch losses. Real failures would stop training or hang.

section: When accumulation or conditional branches enter the picture
question: When using DDP with gradient accumulation over A micro-batches, how should model.no_sync() be used?
options: Around backward only, for the last micro-batch, so that the final gradient is not synchronized
Around both forward and backward for the first A-1 micro-batches; synchronize normally on the last
Around optimizer.step() only, so that the step does not trigger an extra all-reduce of the weights
Around every micro-batch including the last, followed by one manual all-reduce of .grad after the window
explanation: no_sync() suppresses the all-reduce for the micro-batches inside it, so gradients just accumulate locally. Wrapping forward and backward for the first A-1 micro-batches and synchronizing on the last means one all-reduce per optimizer step. If every micro-batch were inside no_sync, gradients would never be averaged.

question: What does a backward pass inside DDP's model.no_sync() context do?
options: It skips computing gradients entirely, so .grad is left unchanged
It skips the all-reduce and just adds the gradient into this rank's .grad
It all-reduces gradients as usual but skips the next optimizer step for the window
It averages gradients only within the local machine, not across nodes
explanation: Inside no_sync(), backward still computes gradients and accumulates them into .grad as usual, but DDP does not launch the all-reduce. The first backward outside the block all-reduces .grad, which already holds the sum of the earlier micro-batches, so one exchange averages the whole window.

question: Why must the forward pass, not just the backward pass, be inside DDP's no_sync() block?
options: Because forward allocates the gradient buffers that no_sync() later frees, so both must be inside
Because DDP's forward prepares the reducer and, inside no_sync(), marks it 'do not communicate'
Because forward performs an all-reduce of activations, which no_sync() must also suppress
Because no_sync() only takes effect on code that creates new tensors, which backward does not
explanation: DDP's forward sets up the reducer that launches all-reduce hooks during backward. The 'skip communication' decision is recorded at forward time inside no_sync(). If only backward is wrapped, the reducer was prepared normally and DDP still synchronizes.

question: With W ranks, A micro-batches per window, each micro-batch loss divided by A, and one all-reduce at the end, what gradient does every rank hold?
options: The sum over all W*A micro-batch gradients, with no averaging applied
The mean over all W*A micro-batch gradients: (1/(W A)) sum_w sum_a g_{w,a}
The mean over the A micro-batches on rank 0 only, which is then broadcast to all ranks
The mean over the W ranks of only the last micro-batch in the window
explanation: Each rank's accumulated gradient is G_w = sum_a g_{w,a}/A, and the final all-reduce averages over ranks, giving (1/W) sum_w G_w = (1/(W A)) sum over all micro-batch gradients. For equal-size micro-batches that is exactly what one big batch would give.

question: If you forget model.no_sync() when accumulating gradients with DDP, what happens?
options: The result is wrong, because the gradients get averaged across ranks A times too many times
Training deadlocks after the first micro-batch, because the ranks wait on mismatched collectives
The result is still correct, but you pay A full-gradient all-reduces per optimizer step instead of one
The gradients are summed across ranks rather than averaged, so they end up W times too large
explanation: Averaging is linear, so averaging each micro-batch's gradient and then adding gives the same final gradient as one average at the end. What changes is cost: every micro-batch triggers a full all-reduce. For a 1B-parameter model with fp32 gradients that is about 4 GB per micro-batch, so A = 8 moves 8 times more data.

question: How much extra memory does DDP's no_sync() cost during gradient accumulation?
options: One extra gradient copy per micro-batch, held until the final synchronizing backward
A communication buffer the size of the activations, allocated once per accumulation window
One extra full copy of the model's parameters, used to store the unsynchronized gradients
None; accumulation happens in the existing .grad tensors, with shape, dtype and device unchanged
explanation: no_sync() does not create tensors; backward just keeps adding into the .grad tensors that already exist. Each .grad keeps its parameter's shape, dtype, and device. Skipping communication saves bandwidth without adding memory.

question: In a DDP accumulation loop, sync_ctx = contextlib.nullcontext() if is_last_in_window else model.no_sync(). What is contextlib.nullcontext() for?
options: It disables gradient computation for that micro-batch, like torch.no_grad()
It is a do-nothing with-block, so the same code synchronizes normally on the last micro-batch
It forces an all-reduce of the loss value on the last micro-batch of each window
It frees the gradient buffers after the optimizer step so the next window starts clean
explanation: nullcontext() is a do-nothing context manager. Choosing between it and no_sync() lets one 'with sync_ctx:' block handle both cases: skip communication on intermediate micro-batches, and synchronize normally on the last one.

question: In a DDP accumulation loop that synchronizes when (i + 1) % A == 0, why do all ranks reach the synchronizing micro-batch at the same i?
options: Because no_sync() aligns the ranks' loop counters before every micro-batch
Because DDP automatically pauses fast ranks until the slow ones catch up
Because DistributedSampler gives every rank the same number of batches
Because the optimizer broadcasts its step index to every rank after each update
explanation: Collectives must be called in matching order on all ranks. DistributedSampler (with drop_last) gives every rank the same number of batches, so the same index i is the end of a window everywhere and all ranks join the same all-reduce together.

question: In a DDP accumulation loop, what happens if len(loader) is not a multiple of A?
options: The leftovers accumulate into .grad without a step; drop them or make the epoch's last batch end a window
DDP raises an error at the end of the epoch, because the ranks' collective counts no longer match
The leftover micro-batches are automatically averaged into the next epoch's first step, with correct scaling
The optimizer steps on each leftover micro-batch individually, using its unaveraged local gradient
explanation: The loop only steps when (i + 1) % A == 0, so trailing micro-batches add into .grad but are never used. With zero_grad placement, they could also leak into the next window. Either drop them or make the last batch of the epoch also end a window.

question: How can you verify that DDP's no_sync() reduces the number of all-reduces during gradient accumulation?
options: Count the optimizer steps per epoch with and without no_sync() and compare the two totals
Compare the loss values and final gradients with and without no_sync() on the same batches
Register a counting comm hook via model.register_comm_hook that increments a counter, then all-reduces
Check torch.cuda.memory_allocated() after each micro-batch, since every all-reduce allocates a buffer
explanation: A communication hook runs whenever DDP reduces a bucket. A counting hook that also performs the all-reduce shows one call per A micro-batches with no_sync() and one per micro-batch without it, for a single-bucket model. The losses and final gradients are the same either way, so they cannot reveal the difference.

question: What can happen in DDP training if one rank skips a backward pass, crashes, or runs out of batches early?
options: DDP silently averages over the remaining ranks
The other ranks automatically continue with W-1 workers
Its peers can be left waiting in a collective
Nothing; collectives are independent per rank
explanation: Collectives require every rank to participate in a compatible sequence. If one rank never issues the matching call, the others block waiting for it, so the job hangs or times out. Investigate the first error across all ranks before retrying.

question: When might a DDP model need find_unused_parameters=True?
options: When the model has branches so some parameters may not receive gradients in a step
Whenever ranks have mismatched training loops or issue different sequences of collectives
Whenever gradient accumulation with no_sync() is used across micro-batches
Whenever the model is larger than 1B parameters and needs many gradient buckets
explanation: Models with conditional branches may leave some parameters unused in a step, and DDP must be told to expect that. The flag is specific to unused parameters; it is not a general fix for ranks with mismatched loops or collective sequences.

question: A single GPU trains with micro-batch 8 and 4 accumulation steps. Moving to 4 GPUs with DDP, both settings are kept. How many examples contribute to each optimizer step before and after?
options: 32 before, 32 after
32 before, 8 after
8 before, 32 after
32 before, 128 after
explanation: Examples per update are micro_batch * accumulation * world_size: 8 * 4 * 1 = 32 before and 8 * 4 * 4 = 128 after. DDP's averaging normalizes the gradient, but it does not cancel the extra examples processed by additional workers.

question: Moving from 1 to 4 GPUs with micro-batch 8, how can you keep the original global batch of 32 examples per optimizer step?
options: Disable DDP's gradient averaging
Multiply the learning rate by 4
Set micro-batch to 32
Set gradient accumulation to 1
explanation: With 4 workers and micro-batch 8, accumulation 1 gives 8 * 1 * 4 = 32. When the worker count grows, one of the other factors must shrink to keep the product constant. Changing the learning rate does not change the number of examples per update.

question: A 4-GPU run processes 128 examples per update while a 1-GPU run processes 32. For equal example exposure, which comparison is fair?
options: 250 updates of the 4-GPU run versus 1,000 of the 1-GPU run
1,000 updates of each run
4,000 updates of the 4-GPU run versus 1,000 of the 1-GPU run
1,000 updates of the 4-GPU run versus 250 of the 1-GPU run
explanation: 1,000 updates at 32 examples is 32,000 examples, and 250 updates at 128 examples is also 32,000. Comparing equal step counts would give the larger-batch run four times the data. For language models, also count valid training tokens.

question: When a change in the number of GPUs changes the global batch size, what should you do about the learning rate?
options: Always multiply it by the GPU count, since the gradient noise falls by exactly that factor
Re-evaluate the learning rate, warmup and schedule; there is no universal multiply-by-GPU rule
Always keep it unchanged, because gradient averaging already makes the step size independent of W
Always divide it by the GPU count, because the averaged gradient is W times larger than before
explanation: A changed global batch can change optimization behavior, so the learning rate, warmup, and schedule should be re-evaluated. There is no universally correct rule like multiplying the learning rate by the GPU count, and a larger batch does not automatically make convergence worse. First decide whether to preserve the original setup or tune a new one.

question: What is wrong with 'all-reduce updates the weights on every worker' as a description of data parallelism?
options: All-reduce combines gradients; the optimizer then updates each local copy of the weights
Nothing; all-reduce averages the weights directly, so that description is exactly right as stated
All-reduce combines activations from the forward pass, not the weights or the gradients
All-reduce only runs on rank 0, which then sends the updated weights to the others
explanation: Confusing gradients with weights is a common mistake. The all-reduce averages gradients; each worker's optimizer then updates its own local replica of the weights using that averaged gradient. No weights are communicated in standard data parallelism.

question: A user wraps the model with DDP and, after loss.backward(), additionally divides every .grad by world_size, believing this is needed to average. What is the effect?
options: The gradients are correct, because default DDP only sums and never divides by W
The gradients are W times too small, because DDP had already averaged them
The gradients become W times too large, because the division is applied before averaging
DDP detects the manual division and skips its own averaging, so the result is unchanged
explanation: Default DDP already averages gradients during backward, so an extra division by W shrinks the gradient by a factor of W. That silently reduces the effective learning rate. The manual all-reduce-and-divide loop explains DDP's job; it is not extra code to add after DDP backward.

question: Why can adding data-parallel workers accidentally change your training setup?
options: Because DDP changes the model architecture by adding synchronization layers to each block
Because more workers reduce the number of trainable parameters stored on each replica
Because DDP automatically lowers the learning rate in proportion to the number of data-parallel workers
Because keeping the local micro-batch and accumulation count fixed increases examples per update
explanation: The global batch is micro_batch * accumulation * world_size, so adding workers with the other two factors fixed increases examples per update. Recalculate all three factors together whenever the worker count changes.

question: Does wrapping a model with DDP make each rank see different training examples?
options: Yes; DDP splits each batch among the ranks automatically when the model is wrapped
No, and having different examples on each rank would break DDP's gradient averaging
Yes, but only on the first epoch; afterwards every rank reverts to the full dataset
No; the input pipeline (e.g. DistributedSampler) must give the workers different samples
explanation: DDP does not choose examples. If every rank loads the same data, they all compute the same gradient and the extra GPUs are wasted. Configure the input pipeline so each worker contributes different samples.

question: With local mean-loss gradients g_w and valid-token counts n_w per data-parallel worker, what is the global token-mean gradient?
options: sum(g_w) / W
sum(n_w * g_w) / W
sum(n_w * g_w) / (W * sum(n_w))
sum(n_w * g_w) / sum(n_w)
explanation: Each g_w is already a mean over n_w tokens, so n_w * g_w recovers the sum over that worker's tokens. Summing those and dividing by the total token count gives the global per-token mean. The default equal worker average sum(g_w)/W only matches when all n_w are equal.

question: What should you do when training with a sum loss under data parallelism?
options: Nothing; averaging the local sums across workers is always equivalent to the global sum
Multiply the learning rate by the global batch size to undo the averaging across workers
Switch the all-reduce to a max, so the largest local sum is used as the global gradient
Decide whether the intended objective is a global sum or a global mean, then scale consistently
explanation: Averaging local sums equals neither the global sum nor the global mean without the appropriate factor. Decide which objective you want and apply the matching scaling. Otherwise the effective learning rate silently depends on W or the batch size.

question: When using mixed-precision gradient scaling together with gradient clipping in data-parallel training, what is the correct order?
options: Clip, then average, then unscale
Average, then unscale, then clip
Unscale, then clip each local gradient, then average
Clip, then unscale, then average
explanation: Clip the gradient the optimizer will actually use: average first, and with a gradient scaler, unscale before clipping so the threshold applies to true gradient magnitudes. Clipping local or still-scaled gradients clips the wrong quantity.

question: Which of these breaks synchronization between data-parallel replicas, even if their gradients match?
options: Different dropout masks on each rank during the forward pass
Different local loss values on each rank at the end of each step
Different optimizer settings or restored optimizer states on each rank
Different training examples on each rank, as drawn by DistributedSampler
explanation: Matching gradients only yield matching updates if optimizer settings, optimizer state, and update counts also match. Different local losses, dropout masks, and data are expected in data parallelism and do not by themselves break synchronization.

question: What happens if data-parallel workers sum their gradients instead of averaging them (equal shards, local mean losses)?
options: The gradient is W times larger than the global mean-loss gradient
Nothing changes, because the optimizer normalizes the gradient's scale
The gradient is W times smaller than the global mean-loss gradient
The workers' weights diverge, because each applies a different update
explanation: For equal shards with mean losses, the average reproduces the global mean-loss gradient, so the sum is W times larger. The replicas still agree, but the effective step size scales with W. Even when averaging, different floating-point reduction orders can cause tiny differences from single-device results.

question: In ring all-reduce of an S-byte tensor across W workers with equal chunks, how many bytes does each worker send?
explanation: Each worker sends W-1 chunks of S/W bytes in each of two phases, for 2(W-1)S/W bytes, and receives the same amount. Each direction approaches 2S as W grows, so sent plus received approaches 4S.

question: Ring all-reduce keeps per-worker bandwidth roughly constant as W grows. Does that make its latency constant too?
options: Yes, the ring finishes in constant time
Yes, because chunks get smaller
No; the ring still has 2(W-1) rounds
No; latency grows as W squared
explanation: Bandwidth accounting shows each worker moves about 2S bytes regardless of W, but the algorithm still runs 2(W-1) sequential rounds. Per-round latency costs therefore grow linearly with W. Bandwidth-optimal does not mean latency-constant.
